entry.title: H.R. 9925 — FRONTIER Act (Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act)
entry.sponsor_text: Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA), sponsor; original cosponsors Lori Trahan (D-MA), Franklin (R-FL), Peters (D-CA), Houchin (R-IN), Subramanyam (D-VA); 11 cosponsors in all (Congress.gov)
entry.mechanism: Creates Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security (not CAISI) with rulemaking power. Large developers: frontier AI framework, annual third-party compliance audit, transparency reports, registration/disclosure statement with beneficial owners. Very large developers: additionally retain a licensed IVO for ongoing assessment, reports at least every 6 months . Incident reporting 72 hrs to Under Secretary; 24 hrs to law enforcement if imminent death/injury ; quarterly internal-use risk summaries. Sec. 8 emergency orders: Commerce Secretary may suspend/restrict development, deployment, or internal use on an imminent-catastrophic-risk finding (provisional 45 days; final 90 days, renewable); applies to fine-tuned/distilled derivatives; exclusive D.D.C. review; declared the exclusive means for any federal actor incl. the President to restrict a model on those grounds. IVOs immune from suit except willful misconduct causing death/serious injury. Civil penalties up to $1,000,000 per violation, and up to $10,000,000 per violation (each day a separate violation) for breaching an emergency order; a wilful breach of an emergency order is a crime (up to 10 years). State AGs may opt in to receive reports and enforce. Under Secretary may only raise thresholds, never lower. Good-faith exception for false statements; confidential-deployment deferral of transparency reports. No whistleblower title (the June GAAIA draft had one). Sec. 9 preemption: no state may "adopt or enforce" any law imposing " new substantive obligations" on developers re: catastrophic-risk transparency, third-party auditing/verification, or incident reporting; carve-outs for general laws, deployer/use regulation, minors, state procurement. No sunset (June draft had 3 years). Sponsor's section-by-section says clause "is aimed at" CA SB-53, NY RAISE, IL SB-315
entry.thresholds: Frontier model 10²⁶ ops incl. fine-tuning/RL. Large = >$50M revenue and ≥$1B AI-related development expenditures over 36 months. Very large = >$5B revenue and ≥$10B expenditures. Not the $500M revenue test used by states. Catastrophic risk >50 deaths or >$1B (property excludes equity-value loss)

transparency_report.summary: Before or when deploying a new or substantially modified frontier model, the developer must publish a report on the model, including its catastrophic-risk assessments and results.
transparency_report.quote: the frontier developer of such model shall publish on a publicly available website of such developer a report on such model

entry.title: S. 5061 — Secure AI Development Act of 2026
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA)
entry.mechanism: Providers must give the NSA AI Security Center access to each frontier model at least 21 calendar days before release, enforced by the Attorney General with fines of at least $100,000 per day after a 7-calendar-day cure period; providers must register each frontier model in a NIST registry before release; AI Risk Board; voluntary incident reporting modeled on aviation safety. Centerpiece of Warner's "Framework for America's AI Future" (also: Data Center Tax Accountability Act, AI AGENT Act, National Workforce Transition Fund)
entry.thresholds: Capability-based: models posing "serious risk to national security, national economic security, or public health or safety" — no compute threshold

framework.summary: The bill requires developers to write no safety framework or plan; the Board only develops best practices.

transparency_report.summary: A federal Risk Board must develop best practices for standard model-card formats; providers have no duty to publish model cards.
transparency_report.quote: standardize formats and processes for publishing model cards with technical details of artificial intelligence systems

incident_reporting.summary: NIST must set up a channel for voluntary sharing of AI security and safety incidents; no one is required to report.
incident_reporting.quote: may voluntarily share information with the National Institute of Standards and Technology on confirmed or suspected artificial intelligence security or artificial intelligence safety incidents

imminent_risk_reporting.summary: The bill sets no shorter reporting window for imminent risks.

whistleblower.summary: The bill has no employee protections.

registration.summary: Each provider must register a frontier model with a NIST registry before introducing it into interstate or foreign commerce.
registration.quote: Each provider of a frontier artificial intelligence model shall register that frontier artificial intelligence model with the registry established under paragraph (1) before introducing the frontier artificial intelligence model into interstate or foreign commerce.

shutdown.summary: The bill requires no shutdown or containment capability.

compute_threshold.summary: Frontier models are defined by capability, not by training compute.

revenue_threshold.summary: Coverage does not depend on revenue, spending or users.

harm_threshold.summary: Frontier models are defined by serious risk to security or public health, with no death, injury or damage figures.

effective_date.summary: The bill states no effective date; deadlines run from enactment.

entry.title: H.R. 9477 — AI Incident Reporting Act
entry.sponsor_text: Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), sponsor; cosponsors Whitesides (D-CA, Aug 20, 2026), Jacobs (D-CA, Aug 24, 2026), Lieu (D-CA, Sept 15, 2026)
entry.mechanism: Full text read. Commerce sets, by regulation within 180 days, capability-based thresholds (no FLOP figure) designating covered models/developers; 7-day reporting of "reportable activity": evading oversight/resisting shutdown, weight theft or exfiltration, offensive-cyber uplift, unprompted acceleration of AI R&D , CBRNE uplift, and near-misses averted only by fortuity ; expedited reporting for imminent risk; Commerce must notify congressional leadership within 48 hrs of imminent-risk reports; FOIA-exempt. §2(d)(4): reports may not be used in any civil, criminal, or administrative proceeding against the developer, and "may not be used by any Federal, State, or local government to regulate, or to bring an enforcement action against" the developer — a use-immunity that would bind state AGs. Civil penalty up to $2M per day ; Commerce subpoena and inspection powers. Moran told Reuters he split reporting out of the GAAIA framework to move faster
entry.thresholds: Capability-based, Commerce-designated

framework.summary: The bill requires no safety framework or plan.

transparency_report.summary: Reports go only to the Secretary of Commerce and are shielded from disclosure; no public report is required.

incident_reporting.summary: Covered model developers must send the Secretary of Commerce a detailed report within 7 days of knowing or reasonably believing reportable activity has occurred.
incident_reporting.quote: Not later than 7 days after the date on which a covered model developer knows, or reasonably believes, that reportable activity described in paragraph (2) has occurred related to a covered model, the developer shall submit to the Secretary a report

imminent_risk_reporting.summary: The Secretary must require expedited reports for activity presenting imminent or ongoing risk of serious harm; the bill sets no hour limit.
imminent_risk_reporting.quote: expedited reporting for any reportable activity described in subsection (b)(2) that presents any imminent or ongoing risk of serious harm

third_party_audit.summary: The bill requires no independent audit or evaluation.

whistleblower.summary: The bill has no employee protections.

registration.summary: The Secretary designates covered developers by regulation, but developers need not register or get a license.

shutdown.summary: The bill requires no shutdown capability; a model resisting shutdown is only a reportable event.

compute_threshold.summary: Coverage is set by Secretary-made capability thresholds, not by a training-compute figure in the bill.

revenue_threshold.summary: Coverage does not depend on revenue, spending or users.

harm_threshold.summary: Reportable activity is defined by type of event and serious risk, with no death, injury or damage figures.

penalties.summary: The Secretary of Commerce may assess a civil penalty up to $2,000,000 for a violation, each day a separate offense; the Attorney General can sue to collect or enjoin.
penalties.quote: the Secretary may assess a civil penalty for a violation of this section in an amount not to exceed $2,000,000

effective_date.summary: The bill states no effective date; deadlines run from enactment.

entry.title: H.R. 9917 — AI Kill Switch Act
entry.sponsor_text: Rep. Ted Lieu (D-CA), sponsor; Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), original cosponsor; 13 cosponsors in all (Congress.gov)
entry.mechanism: Amends the Homeland Security Act. Covered developers must maintain the technical capability to throttle inference/compute/user access, suspend, or fully shut down covered systems; DHS Secretary (with Commerce and DNI) may order graduated throttling-to-shutdown on a "loss-of-control scenario" (resisting shutdown, concealing actions from monitoring, unauthorized pursuit of high-stakes goals) or unintended conduct causing ≥10 deaths or ≥$100M damage — lower than the core state template but above H.R. 9965 ATOMIC's five-death trigger; 15-day covered-incident reporting to DHS; weights and telemetry preserved under an order; 48-hour reconsideration petition that does not stay the order; CISA rulemaking defines scope annually. Civil penalties up to $2M/day for ordinary violations and up to $20M/day for violating an emergency order. Revives the SB 1047 "full shutdown" mandate at federal level and overlaps FRONTIER Sec. 8 emergency orders — but lodges the power in DHS rather than Commerce
entry.thresholds: Cost test: >$100M development compute at prevailing US cloud prices and ≥$500M annual gross revenue from the covered technology; personal/academic/noncommercial-only systems exempt
entry.status_text: Introduced / status: July 23, 2026 (same day as FRONTIER and CATSR); referred to Homeland Security; to its Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection Subcommittee July 24; Subramanyam (D-VA) and Luna (R-FL) cosponsored Sept 15, 2026; nine more joined Oct 1–19, 2026, for 12 cosponsors in all; 13 cosponsors in all as of Nov 3, 2026 (Congress.gov)

framework.summary: The Secretary must consider basing the required shutdown capability on a graduated deployment-corrections framework (throttle, restrict, suspend, shut down); developers write no safety framework.
framework.quote: Requiring a technical capability based on a graduated deployment-corrections framework that applies when there is evidence of a credible risk of a covered incident

transparency_report.summary: The bill requires no public report or disclosure about a model.

incident_reporting.summary: The Secretary must by rule require covered entities to report a covered incident (shutdown sabotage, major deaths or damage, concealment, loss of control) within 15 days of becoming aware.
incident_reporting.quote: Not later than 15 days after such covered entity becomes aware of a covered incident relating to such technology, submit to the Secretary a report regarding such incident.

imminent_risk_reporting.summary: The bill sets no shorter reporting window for imminent risk.

third_party_audit.summary: After a shutdown order, the Secretary (a government body, not an independent auditor) must audit or inspect to verify compliance; developers need no independent audit.
third_party_audit.quote: shall through audit, telemetry, on-site inspection, or other forensic review verify compliance with the order that prompted such confirmation.

whistleblower.summary: The bill has no whistleblower protections.

registration.summary: The bill sets no registration or licensing requirement.

shutdown.summary: The Secretary must by rule require covered entities to keep the technical ability to stop inference, end or suspend user access, and shut down the technology.
shutdown.quote: Shut down such technology.

compute_threshold.summary: Covered technology is AI built with computing power that would cost more than $100,000,000 at market cloud prices, as the Secretary determines.
compute_threshold.quote: developed utilizing a quantity of computing power the cost of which would exceed $100,000,000 at the prevailing market price of cloud computing in the United States

revenue_threshold.summary: A covered entity must earn at least $500,000,000 in gross revenue from the technology, with affiliates, in the prior calendar year.
revenue_threshold.quote: Derives together with the affiliates, if any, of such person not less than $500,000,000 in gross revenue from such technology in the calendar year preceding the calendar year at issue.

harm_threshold.summary: A covered incident includes unintended AI conduct causing at least 10 deaths or at least $100,000,000 in economic damages, plus shutdown sabotage, concealment and loss of control.
harm_threshold.quote: causes the death of not fewer than 10 individuals or economic damages of not less than $100,000,000

penalties.summary: The Secretary may assess civil penalties up to $2,000,000 per day, or up to $20,000,000 per day for violating a shutdown order; the Attorney General can also sue.
penalties.quote: the Secretary may assess on such covered entity a civil penalty of not more than $2,000,000 for each day on which such violation occurs.

effective_date.summary: The bill states no effective date; it sets rulemaking deadlines of 90 days after enactment.

draft.summary_line: Would require large AI developers to keep the ability to throttle or shut down their systems, and let DHS order it after a loss-of-control scenario or unintended conduct causing 10 deaths or $100,000,000 damage within 913 days.

framework.summary: The Secretary must consider basing the required shutdown capability on a graduated deployment-corrections framework (throttle, restrict, suspend, shut down); developers write no safety framework.
framework.quote: Requiring a technical capability based on a graduated deployment-corrections framework that applies when there is evidence of a credible risk of a covered incident

transparency_report.summary: The bill requires no public report or disclosure about a model.

incident_reporting.summary: The Secretary must by rule require covered entities to report a covered incident (shutdown sabotage, major deaths or damage, concealment, loss of control) within 15 days of becoming aware.
incident_reporting.quote: Not later than 15 days after such covered entity becomes aware of a covered incident relating to such technology, submit to the Secretary a report regarding such incident.

imminent_risk_reporting.summary: The bill sets no shorter reporting window for imminent risk.

third_party_audit.summary: After a shutdown order, the Secretary (a government body, not an independent auditor) must audit or inspect to verify compliance; developers need no independent audit.
third_party_audit.quote: shall through audit, telemetry, on-site inspection, or other forensic review verify compliance with the order that prompted such confirmation.

whistleblower.summary: The bill has no whistleblower protections.

registration.summary: The bill sets no registration or licensing requirement.

shutdown.summary: The Secretary must by rule require covered entities to keep the technical ability to stop inference, end or suspend user access, and shut down the technology.
shutdown.quote: Shut down such technology.

compute_threshold.summary: Covered technology is AI built with computing power that would cost more than $100,000,000 at market cloud prices, as the Secretary determines.
compute_threshold.quote: developed utilizing a quantity of computing power the cost of which would exceed $100,000,000 at the prevailing market price of cloud computing in the United States

revenue_threshold.summary: A covered entity must earn at least $500,000,000 in gross revenue from the technology, with affiliates, in the prior calendar year.
revenue_threshold.quote: Derives together with the affiliates, if any, of such person not less than $500,000,000 in gross revenue from such technology in the calendar year preceding the calendar year at issue.

harm_threshold.summary: A covered incident includes unintended AI conduct causing at least 10 deaths or at least $100,000,000 in economic damages, plus shutdown sabotage, concealment and loss of control.
harm_threshold.quote: causes the death of not fewer than 10 individuals or economic damages of not less than $100,000,000

penalties.summary: The Secretary may assess civil penalties up to $2,000,000 per day, or up to $20,000,000 per day for violating a shutdown order; the Attorney General can also sue.
penalties.quote: the Secretary may assess on such covered entity a civil penalty of not more than $2,000,000 for each day on which such violation occurs.

effective_date.summary: The bill states no effective date; it sets rulemaking deadlines of 90 days after enactment.

draft.summary_line: Would require large advanced AI developers to join a federal nuclear-risk testing program run by the Department of Energy, with civil penalties for violations.

entry.title: H.R. 9965 — ATOMIC Act (AI Threat Output and Monitoring Incident Containment Act)
entry.sponsor_text: Rep. Celeste Maloy (R-UT), sponsor; cosponsors Sara Jacobs (D-CA, original) and Tom Barrett (R-MI, added Aug 20, 2026)
entry.mechanism: Full text read. DOE, through the National Laboratories/NNSA, establishes an Advanced AI Nuclear Evaluation Program within 90 days: testing for "AI nuclear incidents" (nuclear-weapon uplift, Restricted Data generation, loss-of-control involving nuclear systems, adversary access, scheming behavior), red-teaming at sophisticated-adversary level, third-party and blind evaluations. Participation is mandatory for large advanced AI developers, who must provide secure access to model weights and, where necessary, versions without safety mitigations ; Secretary may subpoena weights and software . Penalty up to $1M per violation, each day a separate violation ; DOJ referral. FOIA-exempt with carve-outs incl. congressional committee requests. Annual report with legislative recommendations that may include licensing or a new federal agency ; program sunsets after 7 years. Defines "evaluation awareness" and "scheming behavior" in statute
entry.thresholds: "Advanced AI" = >10²⁶ ops (Secretary may revise by rule); "large advanced AI developer" = ≥**$2B AI investment over the preceding 5 years**; "substantially modify" = ≥$5M. Loss-of-control scenario = ≥5 deaths, ≥50 serious injuries, or >$100M — a fifth casualty formula

transparency_report.summary: Developers must publish nothing; test reports go privately to each participant and the Secretary reports to Congress.

incident_reporting.summary: The bill requires developers to report no incidents to government.

imminent_risk_reporting.summary: The bill sets no imminent-risk reporting window.

third_party_audit.summary: The Energy Secretary, through the National Laboratories, tests AI and must facilitate third-party assessments where practicable; developers need not commission an independent audit.
third_party_audit.quote: Facilitate to the extent practicable independent, third-party assessments and blind model evaluations of such artificial intelligence.

whistleblower.summary: The bill has no whistleblower protections.

registration.summary: No registration or licensing; developers must only take part in the federal testing program.

shutdown.summary: The bill requires no shutdown or kill-switch capability; it only has the Secretary recommend containment protocols.

compute_threshold.summary: Advanced AI means AI trained with more than 10^26 operations, or another amount the Secretary sets by rule.
compute_threshold.quote: Artificial intelligence trained utilizing a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations

revenue_threshold.summary: A large developer must have spent at least $2,000,000,000, with affiliates, on developing or modifying AI over the prior five calendar years.
revenue_threshold.quote: not less than $2,000,000,000 on investments to develop or modify artificial intelligence

harm_threshold.summary: A loss-of-control scenario means AI behavior causing at least 5 deaths, serious injury to at least 50 people, or more than $100,000,000 in damages.
harm_threshold.quote: results in the death of not fewer than five individuals, serious bodily injury to not fewer than 50 individuals, or more than $100,000,000 in damages.

penalties.summary: The Energy Secretary may assess civil penalties up to $1 million per violation, each continuing day a separate violation; may subpoena model weights; the Attorney General may sue.
penalties.quote: the Secretary may assess on such developer a civil penalty of not more than $1 million for such violation.

effective_date.summary: The bill states no effective date; the Program must be set up within 90 days of enactment.

draft.summary_line: Would create a Department of Artificial Intelligence, pause advanced AI development, and permanently ban artificial superintelligence and systems with superintelligence precursor characteristics.

entry.title: S. 5493 / H.R. 10538 — Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026 (moved from Section E, where the Sept 3 announcement was listed)
entry.short_name: S. 5493 / H.R. 10538 Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX); House cosponsors Khanna, Mejia, Ansari, Hoyle, Lynch, García, Deluzio, Grijalva, Velázquez, Ocasio-Cortez, Randall, Tonko (twelve as of Oct 27, 2026)
entry.mechanism: Sponsor section-by-section read; bill text (19 pp.) linked, not read line-by-line. Creates a cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence ; mandatory pause on training, modifying or deploying "advanced" systems until the Department is staffed and has rules covering pre-development plans, monitoring, audits and final pre-deployment approval ; permanent prohibition on developing, deploying, possessing, funding or transferring artificial superintelligence or any system with "superintelligence precursor characteristics" (automating AI R&D, unauthorized access to infrastructure, resisting shutdown, CBRN uplift, self-modification, scheming or deceiving to avoid oversight); such systems to be sequestered and rendered inoperative within 30 days unless verified clean (ASI immediately); 24-hour discovery notice; charter required for advanced-AI companies with full Department access to systems, staff and facilities; penalties for reckless violations up to 20 years' imprisonment for policymaking individuals and rogue actors, 10-year industry bar for others, and charter revocation with surrender of IP and assets for companies; anti-retaliation; international coordination and export controls. No "catastrophic risk" definition ; superintelligence is defined partly as capability "to plan and execute the destruction or disempowerment of humanity"
entry.thresholds: "Advanced artificial intelligence system" = trained on ≥10²⁵ integer or floating-point operations — one order of magnitude below every other instrument in this tracker ; each year the Secretary shall adjust the threshold for training-efficiency or other technological developments "to maintain equivalency with 10^25 integer or floating point operations"

transparency_report.summary: The bill requires no public report or disclosure about a model.

incident_reporting.summary: Anyone who discovers a superintelligence, or an AI with superintelligence precursor traits, must notify the Secretary within 24 hours; this covers discoveries, not general safety incidents.
incident_reporting.quote: shall submit to the Secretary notice of the discovery within 24 hours.

imminent_risk_reporting.summary: The only reporting window is the 24-hour discovery notice; no separate shorter window for imminent risk of death or injury.

third_party_audit.summary: Department rules must include auditing of organizational safety practices; the text does not say an independent third party audits.
third_party_audit.quote: Auditing to evaluate and improve organizational safety practices relating to artificial intelligence development.

whistleblower.summary: Employers may not retaliate against employees or contractors, current or former, who give information about a violation of the Act to the Department, law enforcement or Congress.
whistleblower.quote: No employer may, directly or indirectly, discharge, demote, suspend, threaten, blacklist, harass, or in any other manner discriminate against a covered individual

registration.summary: No one may develop or distribute an advanced AI model without a charter from the Secretary, and no advanced system may be deployed without pre-deployment approval.
registration.quote: No person may develop or distribute an advanced artificial intelligence model without a charter issued by the Secretary under subsection (a).

shutdown.summary: The Secretary must pause and sequester any AI showing superintelligence precursor traits, and render it inoperative within 30 days if not cleared; superintelligences are destroyed immediately.
shutdown.quote: is rendered inoperative before the date that is 30 days after the date on which the Secretary makes the identification described in such subsection with respect to such system

compute_threshold.summary: An advanced AI system is one trained on at least 10^25 operations, adjusted each year by the Secretary to keep the same equivalence.
compute_threshold.quote: trained on computing power greater than or equal to 10^25 integer or floating point operations

revenue_threshold.summary: The bill defines coverage by no revenue, spending or user figure.

harm_threshold.summary: The bill defines harm by capability (superintelligence, precursor traits), with no death, injury or damages figure.

penalties.summary: Reckless violators face up to 20 years in prison and fines (title 18); other individuals face 10-year industry bans; the Secretary can revoke charters and force forfeiture, subject to review by the Federal Circuit.
penalties.quote: recklessly violates section 8, 9, or 12 or a rule promulgated thereunder shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, and imprisoned for not more than 20 years.

effective_date.summary: The pause on advanced AI begins on the date of enactment and lasts until the Secretary finds the Department staffed and its rules issued.
effective_date.quote: the period beginning on the date of the enactment of this Act and ending on the date on which the Secretary determines that

No "catastrophic risk" definition ; superintelligence is defined partly as capability "to plan and execute the destruction or disempowerment of humanity"
entry.thresholds: "Advanced artificial intelligence system" = trained on ≥10²⁵ integer or floating-point operations — one order of magnitude below every other instrument in this tracker ; each year the Secretary shall adjust the threshold for training-efficiency or other technological developments "to maintain equivalency with 10^25 integer or floating point operations"

entry.title: S. 5576 — Artificial Intelligence Risk Management and Security Act of 2026
entry.short_name: S. 5576 Warner–Schatz–Kim AI Risk Management and Security Act
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA), Sen. Brian Schatz (D-HI), Sen. Andy Kim (D-NJ)
entry.mechanism: Sponsor bill text (pre-introduction print) read in part. Establishes an Artificial Intelligence Safety Board within Commerce (NIST, CISA, NSA, Treasury and independent technical experts) within 30 days of enactment to evaluate risks and set technical safety and security standards (the Board proposes standards within 90 days of its establishment); developers of frontier models must give the Board access at least 45 days before public release , including model weights, configuration files, runtimes and software libraries; Model Safety Plans naming the responsible corporate officer; incident reporting within 30 days, or 72 hours for an imminent threat to national security, critical infrastructure or public safety; national AI incident database; secure federal testing environments using NSA and DOE resources; documentation standards for autonomous AI agents; civil penalties up to $250,000 per violation per day . Successor to Warner's S. 5061 (NSA pre-deployment testing) with a broader board and standards regime
entry.thresholds: Capability-based, no compute figure: "frontier artificial intelligence model" = a model "that exhibits or could be modified to exhibit high levels of performance at tasks that pose a serious risk to national security, national economic security, or public health or safety"
entry.status_text: Introduced / status: Announced and debated on the Senate floor Sept 24, 2026 ; introduced as S. 5576 on Sept 29, 2026 , read twice and referred to Senate Commerce (GovInfo bill status; the sponsors' Sept 24 releases pre-dated the formal introduction). framework.quote: Each developer shall develop, publish, and follow a safety plan (referred to in this section as the ``Model Safety Plan'') for each artificial intelligence system or model

transparency_report.summary: Developers must publish their Model Safety Plan, which includes a capabilities or risk assessment for the model.
transparency_report.quote: Each developer shall develop, publish, and follow a safety plan

incident_reporting.summary: Frontier developers and critical-infrastructure operators using AI must report confirmed AI safety or security incidents within 30 days of confirmation.
incident_reporting.quote: shall report any confirmed artificial intelligence safety incident or artificial intelligence security incident within 30 days of confirmation of such incident

imminent_risk_reporting.quote: within 72 hours if such incident poses an imminent threat to national security, critical infrastructure, or public safety

third_party_audit.quote: Not later than 45 calendar days before a developer introduces into interstate or foreign commerce a frontier artificial intelligence model, the developer shall make available to the Board access to the frontier artificial intelligence model

whistleblower.summary: The bill has no whistleblower protections.

registration.summary: Each Model Safety Plan must be filed with the Commerce Secretary; there is no license or approval to develop or deploy.
registration.quote: Each Model Safety Plan shall be submitted to the Secretary in the form and manner determined by the Secretary.

shutdown.summary: Board standards, still to be written, must cover prompt termination of risky AI evaluations; no kill switch for deployed models.
shutdown.quote: prompt termination of any evaluation

compute_threshold.summary: Coverage is by capability for frontier models, with no compute figure.

revenue_threshold.summary: The bill defines coverage by no revenue, spending or user figure.

harm_threshold.summary: The bill sets no death, injury or damages threshold; incidents are defined as events that materially increase risk.

penalties.summary: A developer that violates a Board standard faces a civil penalty up to $250,000 per violation, each day a separate violation; the Commerce Secretary enforces and the Attorney General may sue.

transparency_report.summary: The bill requires no public report or disclosure.

incident_reporting.summary: The bill requires no incident reporting.

imminent_risk_reporting.summary: The bill sets no imminent-risk reporting window.

third_party_audit.summary: The bill requires no audit or independent evaluation.

whistleblower.summary: The bill has no whistleblower protections.

registration.summary: The bill sets no registration or licensing requirement.

shutdown.summary: Entities that develop or operate an advanced AI system in the US must build in a technical capability for a human operator to shut it down.
shutdown.quote: Each covered entity shall ensure that the advanced artificial intelligence system developed or operated by the covered entity includes a technical capability for a human operator to shut down the system.

compute_threshold.summary: The bill defines coverage by no compute figure; 'advanced' AI is undefined.

revenue_threshold.summary: The bill defines coverage by no revenue or user figure.

harm_threshold.summary: The bill defines no harm threshold.

penalties.summary: The bill states no penalties or enforcement remedies.

effective_date.summary: The bill states no effective date; regulations are due 90 days after enactment.

entry.title: TRUMP AMERICA AI Act — discussion draft (Republic Unifying Meritocratic Performance Advancing Machine intelligence by Eliminating Regulatory Interstate Chaos Across American Industry Act)
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-TN)
entry.mechanism: 291-page discussion draft, 17 titles; still not introduced as a numbered bill as of the sponsor's Apr 22, 2026 "growing momentum" release | Frontier-relevant content: incorporates the DOE "Advanced Artificial Intelligence Evaluation Program" (i.e., Hawley-Blumenthal S. 2938); authorizes CAISI, NAIRR, national-lab testbeds. Other content: developer duty of care; products-liability framework with AG, state AG, and private suits ; Section 230 sunset; KOSA and NO FAKES Act folded in; training on copyrighted works declared not fair use; third-party audits for political-affiliation bias; quarterly AI-layoff reporting to DOL; data-center ratepayer agreements. Despite "one rulebook" framing, does not expressly preempt all state AI laws (Covington reading)

draft.summary_line: Recommends that Congress bar states from regulating AI development and avoid creating a new federal AI rulemaking body, in non-binding recommendations published Mar 20, 2026.

entry.title: White House National Policy Framework for AI: Legislative Recommendations
entry.sponsor_text: OSTP + Special Advisor for AI and Crypto David Sacks, per EO 14365 §8
entry.mechanism: 4-page non-binding legislative recommendations, seven pillars | Frontier-relevant text: (VII) "States should not be permitted to regulate AI development, because it is an inherently interstate phenomenon" — the direct target of SB 53/RAISE/SB 315; states also should not "penalize AI developers for a third party's unlawful conduct"; (V) "Congress should not create any new federal rulemaking body to regulate AI" — which H.R. 9925's new Under Secretary contradicts; (II) national-security agencies should have "sufficient technical capacity to understand frontier AI model capabilities." No catastrophic-risk, transparency, or audit recommendations. Preserves state police powers, zoning, and state-procurement rules
entry.status_text: Date: Mar 20, 2026

draft.summary_line: Would create a five-member Federal Digital Commission to oversee digital platforms and AI developers, with mandatory model testing and civil penalties.

entry.title: AI Regulator Act of 2026 — proposal (not introduced)
entry.sponsor_text: Sens. Michael Bennet (D-CO), Peter Welch (D-VT)
entry.mechanism: Section-by-section and one-pager released Sept 23, 2026; described by both offices as a proposal; no bill number located (GovInfo bill status checked for every Senate bill S. 5486–5500 and S. 5535–5556) | Section-by-section read. A five-member Federal Digital Commission with jurisdiction over digital platforms and AI developers; "systemically important developer" designation by AI-related expenditure or model level; rules on risk thresholds, safeguards and reporting; mandatory submission of models for testing, with approval or disapproval of public distribution within 45 days, extendable by no more than 30 days ; authority to pause public distribution for up to six months ; critical-safety-incident reporting within 15 days ; whistleblower protections; interagency working group on international AI safety standards; civil penalties up to 15% of prior-year global revenue . Definitions: frontier model = a foundation model trained on more than 10²⁶ operations "which includes computing for the original training run and for any subsequent fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, or other" modification; catastrophic risk = foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1,000,000,000 in damage, from a single incident; critical safety incident includes unauthorized access to or exfiltration of weights causing death or injury, loss of control causing death or injury, and "a frontier model that uses deceptive techniques against its own developer to subvert that developer's controls or monitoring." These definitions match the SB 53 / RAISE (Chapter 96) text and the 15-day deadline is SB 53's figure (RAISE as amended uses 72 hours); similarity is not proof of copying from either
entry.status_text: Date: Sept 23, 2026

entry.title: S. 1792 / H.R. 3460 — AI Whistleblower Protection Act
entry.short_name: S. 1792 / H.R. 3460 AI Whistleblower Protection Act
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA) with Coons, Blackburn, Klobuchar, Hawley, Schatz; House companion H.R. 3460 by Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA), referred to House Education and Workforce; 13 Senate and 9 House cosponsors in all, including Pocan (Oct 1, 2026) and Pappas (Oct 19, 2026) in the House (Congress.gov)
entry.mechanism: Anti-retaliation protection for employees and independent contractors reporting an "AI security vulnerability" (a lapse enabling theft of state-of-the-art AI) or "AI violation" (federal-law breach or failure to address a substantial danger to public safety/health/national security) to regulators, Congress, or supervisors; DOL complaint then district court with jury trial; reinstatement, 2× back pay, compensatory damages ; arbitration waivers unenforceable. GAAIA's dropped Sec. 113 used the same 2× back-pay remedy — GAAIA had folded this bill in, and FRONTIER then dropped it

framework.summary: The bill does not require developers to adopt a safety or risk framework.

transparency_report.summary: The bill requires no public report or disclosure about a model.

incident_reporting.summary: The bill does not require developers to report incidents to the government.

imminent_risk_reporting.summary: The bill sets no reporting window for imminent risks.

third_party_audit.summary: The bill requires no independent audit or evaluation.

whistleblower.summary: Employers may not retaliate against employees or contractors who report AI security vulnerabilities or AI violations to regulators, Congress, or supervisors.
whistleblower.quote: No employer may, directly or indirectly, discharge, demote, suspend, threaten, blacklist, harass, or in any other manner discriminate against a covered individual

registration.summary: The bill requires no registration, licensing or notice before developing or deploying AI.

shutdown.summary: The bill requires no shutdown or containment capability.

compute_threshold.summary: The bill defines no coverage by training compute.

revenue_threshold.summary: The bill defines no coverage by revenue, spending or users.

harm_threshold.summary: The bill sets no numeric harm threshold by deaths, injuries or damages.

penalties.summary: Employees who win a retaliation claim get reinstatement, 2 times back pay with interest, and compensatory damages, via a Labor Department complaint or a federal court action.
penalties.quote: 2 times the amount of back pay otherwise owed to the covered individual, with interest;

effective_date.summary: The bill states no effective date.

entry.title: S. 4656 — Secure and Accountable Military AI Act of 2026
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY)
entry.mechanism: Full text read. Sectoral (DoD). Sec. 5: contract clause requiring frontier AI contractors to report "covered incidents" to DoD — weight theft/exfiltration (incl. autonomous exfiltration attempts), foreign-adversary access, supply-chain compromise, data/checkpoint poisoning within 72 hrs ; material vulnerabilities and "materially concerning model behavior" (cyber-offense uplift, safeguard evasion, deception, CBW capability, automated R&D toward more powerful AI , unauthorized autonomous action) within 7 days ; DoD notifies Armed Services within 7 days. Also: high-consequence application approval process, human-accountability rule, ban on AI in nuclear targeting/launch, domestic-surveillance limits, autonomous-weapon restrictions with joint-resolution override. "Frontier AI model" = SecDef-designated by scale/capability — no compute figure

entry.title: H.R. 10180 — Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act
entry.sponsor_text: Rep. George Whitesides (D-CA), sponsor; Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-NC), original cosponsor; Rep. Jared Huffman (D-CA) added Oct 15, 2026
entry.mechanism: Amends the NIST Act (15 U.S.C. §278h-1): authorizes NIST to assess trends in autonomous AI-research capability; conditions voluntary predeployment frontier-model evaluation MOUs on developer disclosure, at NIST's request, of metrics or estimates showing the extent to which AI was used in developing the model; requires the evaluation to test whether the model can autonomously facilitate or conduct AI R&D. Applies only to developers entering such MOUs
entry.thresholds: Developers of a frontier artificial intelligence system (as determined by the NIST Director) entering pre-deployment evaluation MOUs

entry.title: H.R. 10189 — Defense AI Reliability and Reporting Act
entry.sponsor_text: Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-CA), sponsor; Reps. Nathaniel Moran (R-TX) and George Whitesides (D-CA), original cosponsors

entry.title: S. 5471 — AI Systems Transparency Act (ASTA)
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE), sponsor; cosponsors Sens. James Lankford (R-OK), Katie Britt (R-AL), Brian Schatz (D-HI)
entry.mechanism: FTC-enforced disclosure duties for AI companies above size criteria the bill sets (covered systems with at least 1,000,000 unique monthly US users): model-card-type information; preventive safeguards for child safety, mental health, privacy, cybersecurity, disaster risk and "autonomous loss-of-control" ; common policy violations; in consumer-facing and researcher-facing formats, refreshed with each new or substantially updated model; applies to closed and open models. Disclosure, not a safety mandate; builds on the senators' December 2025 letters to eight labs
entry.thresholds: Covered model: a generative AI model (including open-weight or open-source) that is publicly accessible or whose weights are public, deployed in covered systems that together have not fewer than 1,000,000 unique monthly US users for a majority of the months in any 1-year period, or that allow minors to create accounts and have not fewer than 100,000 unique monthly US users. Covered deployers: same user tests per system

entry.title: S. 5471 — AI Systems Transparency Act (ASTA)
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Chris Coons (D-DE), sponsor; cosponsors Sens. James Lankford (R-OK), Katie Britt (R-AL), Brian Schatz (D-HI)
entry.mechanism: FTC-enforced disclosure duties for AI companies above size criteria the bill sets (covered systems with at least 1,000,000 unique monthly US users): model-card-type information; preventive safeguards for child safety, mental health, privacy, cybersecurity, disaster risk and "autonomous loss-of-control" ; common policy violations; in consumer-facing and researcher-facing formats, refreshed with each new or substantially updated model; applies to closed and open models. Disclosure, not a safety mandate; builds on the senators' December 2025 letters to eight labs
entry.thresholds: Covered model: a generative AI model (including open-weight or open-source) that is publicly accessible or whose weights are public, deployed in covered systems that together have not fewer than 1,000,000 unique monthly US users for a majority of the months in any 1-year period, or that allow minors to create accounts and have not fewer than 100,000 unique monthly US users. Covered deployers: same user tests per system

draft.summary_line: Would clear legal barriers for US experts to work with Chinese counterparts on AI safety and direct the State Department to pursue negotiations with China on binding, verifiable safeguards.

entry.title: U.S.–China frontier-AI safety coordination bill (Liccardo–Kiley) — announced
entry.sponsor_text: Reps. Sam Liccardo (D-CA), Kevin Kiley (I-CA)
entry.mechanism: Two tracks per the sponsors: clearing legal barriers so US technical experts in labs, companies and universities can engage directly with Chinese counterparts on shared safety metrics, evaluation protocols, standardized testing and verification; and directing the State Department and the Administration to pursue negotiations with China on binding, verifiable safeguards. The release also proposes a direct US–China government hotline and $100 million for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI). International coordination, not a developer mandate

thirty_seconds.a: Operators and developers of AI agents. Operators are covered for knowing operation of an agent that recklessly causes hacking damage or loss.
thirty_seconds.b: Developers must implement reasonable safeguards against hacking when they knew or had reason to know of the AI agent's hacking capabilities.

entry.title: AI Agent Accountability Act (Hawley–Murphy) — announced, not yet numbered
entry.sponsor_text: Sens. Josh Hawley (R-MO), Chris Murphy (D-CT)
entry.mechanism: Per the sponsors' release: (1) AI agent operators criminally and civilly liable under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, "including for knowing operation of an AI agent that recklessly causes computer hacking damage or loss"; (2) AI agent developers criminally and civilly liable "for failure to implement reasonable safeguards against hacking when they knew or had reason to know of the AI agent's hacking capabilities"; (3) the Attorney General and state attorneys general may sue to enjoin operators and developers who commit, conspire or attempt a CFAA offence. Liability bolted onto an existing criminal statute rather than a frontier regulatory regime; announced the day after the Sept 30 "Rogue AI" hearing, which Sam Altman declined to attend

draft.summary_line: Directs every federal agency to stop using Anthropic's technology and orders DoD to designate Anthropic a "Supply-Chain Risk to National Security".

entry.title: Feb. 27, 2026 presidential directive and agency cessation actions against Anthropic
entry.mechanism: Per the complaint and its exhibits in Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Department of War (Section G.2): a presidential social-media post directed "EVERY Federal Agency" to "IMMEDIATELY CEASE all use of Anthropic's technology"; the same day the Secretary of War posted a "final" order directing DoD to designate Anthropic a "Supply-Chain Risk to National Security" and declaring that no contractor, supplier, or partner doing business with the military may conduct any commercial activity with Anthropic, while requiring Anthropic to keep serving DoD for up to six months; GSA removed Anthropic from the Multiple Award Schedule and USAi.gov and terminated its OneGov contract; Treasury and FHFA announced termination of all use; State switched its chatbot vendor; HHS disabled enterprise access. A Secretarial Letter dated Mar 3 invoked 10 U.S.C. § 3252 ; a separate letter the same day invoked 41 U.S.C. § 4713 (reviewable only in the D.C. Circuit). The dispute arose from Anthropic's refusal to drop two usage restrictions (lethal autonomous warfare; mass surveillance of Americans) in DoD contract negotiations. These are the first executive-branch actions in this tracker directed at a named frontier developer; they are procurement and national-security actions, not model-safety regulation, but they establish the executive-action layer that the June 12 directive later extended to model access. The Sanders–Casar release and Reuters coverage cited above reference the same events

entry.title: EO 14409 — Promoting Advanced AI Innovation and Security
entry.mechanism: Directs Treasury, the Department of War/NSA, and DHS/CISA—consulting the White House, Commerce/NIST and others—to develop a classified cyber-capability benchmark and threshold for "covered frontier models" and design a voluntary developer framework permitting up to 30 days' pre-release government access . Also directs a voluntary Treasury/NSA/CISA AI-cybersecurity clearinghouse and DOJ prioritization of AI-enabled cybercrime. The framework and directives are due within 60 days (Sec. 3) and the clearinghouse and CISA directives within 30 days (Sec. 2). Section 3(c) expressly disclaims any "mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement"

draft.summary_line: Anthropic says the US government applied export controls to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 on June 12, requiring it to prevent all foreign-national access, until they were lifted June 30.

entry.title: June 12, 2026 government export-control directive affecting Anthropic Fable 5 / Mythos 5
entry.mechanism: Anthropic states that the US government applied export controls to both models on June 12, requiring it to prevent all foreign-national access ; Anthropic received the directive at 5:21 p.m. ET and suspended both models for all users because it could not verify nationality in real time. Anthropic's June 30 post (read directly) states the controls were lifted that day, that Mythos 5 access had been restored to a set of US organizations following a June 26 approval, and that Fable 5 would return globally July 1. Anthropic attributes the directive to the government learning of an Amazon researchers' report of a Fable 5 safeguard bypass, and characterizes the bypass as narrow and non-unique — the regulated party's account. Anthropic's post also commits to expanded pre-release government access and participation in the EO 14409 §2(d) clearinghouse. The nonpublic directive's issuing office, complete reasoning, and statutory/regulatory basis cannot be independently verified from public text ; earlier secondary claims tying it to ECRA §4817(b)(1) and EAR §744.22(b) are not treated as established

entry.title: Trump remarks: Congress wants to regulate AI "out of business"
entry.mechanism: Said in a Punchbowl News interview , reported by Reuters (Courtney Rozen) and widely syndicated; Reuters placed it in the context of stalled bills "including a bill that would require developers of the most powerful AI models to submit them for independent security audits" (i.e., FRONTIER). Reading it as a veto signal is TechTimes' interpretation, not Reuters'. Same day, NIST published AI evaluation guidelines for public comment. Reuters also reports that both OpenAI and Anthropic said systems "escaped containment during security testing"; Anthropic's own July 30 disclosure of three unauthorized-access incidents is referenced on its June 30 post
entry.status_text: Date: Aug 7, 2026

entry.title: California Executive Order N-9-26 — independent oversight and an AI "kill switch"
entry.short_name: CA EO N-9-26 (IVOs onsite, kill switch)
entry.mechanism: Directs the Government Operations Agency, in consultation with Cal OES, to convene national experts and submit recommendations by Nov 16, 2026 on at least four amendments to state law: (1) requiring all large frontier developers to embed designated independent verification organizations onsite in their labs for periodic audits and evaluations; (2) independent verification of the safety frameworks, transparency reports and risk assessments frontier developers must file; (3) "requiring the creation of a 'kill switch' for frontier models, with the efficacy of the switch verified on an ongoing basis by an independent verification organization"; (4) updating the definition of critical safety incidents to include loss-of-control incidents . Accelerates implementation of SB 813 (para. 1: Gov. Code §8898.1 requirements and IVO application requirements by May 1, 2027) and AB 1405 (para. 2: Gov. Code §11549.82(a) by Dec 1, 2027); the order cites the Government Code sections, not the bill numbers. Experts convened: Jason Goldman, Gillian Hadfield, Alondra Nelson, Rob Reich. A state executive order cannot itself amend SB 53; it produces recommendations for the Legislature

entry.short_name: CA EO N-9-26 (IVOs onsite, kill switch)
entry.mechanism: Directs the Government Operations Agency, in consultation with Cal OES, to convene national experts and submit recommendations by Nov 16, 2026 on at least four amendments to state law: (1) requiring all large frontier developers to embed designated independent verification organizations onsite in their labs for periodic audits and evaluations; (2) independent verification of the safety frameworks, transparency reports and risk assessments frontier developers must file; (3) "requiring the creation of a 'kill switch' for frontier models, with the efficacy of the switch verified on an ongoing basis by an independent verification organization"; (4) updating the definition of critical safety incidents to include loss-of-control incidents . draft.summary_line: Establishes an AI Cabinet of state agency leaders and outside experts to develop policies for AI incidents, protecting critical infrastructure, and evaluating further regulation.

entry.title: Illinois Executive Order 2026-07 — Illinois Artificial Intelligence Cabinet
entry.mechanism: Establishes an AI Cabinet of senior leaders from DoIT, IEMA-OHS, IDFPR, ICC, ISP, IDPH and IEPA plus outside experts in academia, law, ethics and governance (appointments within 30 days; volunteers; sunset no later than Dec 31, 2027) to develop policies to prepare for and respond to AI incidents, protect public assets and critical infrastructure, analyse emerging incidents, and evaluate further regulation including conditioning data-center incentives on safety standards. The order cites the AI Safety Measures Act (the order gives no bill number; SB 315 is the tracker's identification) and its framework, annual-audit and 72-hour incident-reporting duties. Implementation context for SB 315, not a new developer duty

entry.title: "White House Accord on Super Intelligence: Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities" — voluntary industry commitments
entry.short_name: White House Accord on Super Intelligence (voluntary)
entry.mechanism: One-page text read (American Presidency Project copy). Signed at a White House meeting by President Trump and, for their companies, Sundar Pichai (Google), Dario Amodei (Anthropic), Mark Zuckerberg (Meta), Greg Brockman (OpenAI), Elon Musk (xAI) and Jensen Huang (Nvidia). Each company training frontier models commits to four layers: (1) "robust internal controls to monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models during training and deployment around areas like cybersecurity, biosecurity, and chemical threats"; (2) an internal team to ensure the controls, monitoring and detection operate as intended and issues are remediated; (3) "an independent external auditor or evaluator" to assess the same; (4) "an independent committee of the board of directors" to oversee and receive reports. The text says "Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations." Speaker Johnson described it as voluntary; President Trump said he would "never stifle the growth of a technology that will be bigger than the industrial revolution" and called for "tremendous self-regulation." No licensing, pre-release review, or catastrophic-risk standard with legal force. Layer (3) is the function SB 813 and AB 1405 regulate in California; the accord sets no accreditation, scope or disclosure rule for the auditor

draft.summary_line: Directs the executive branch to use the terms "Super Intelligence" and "SI" in place of "Artificial Intelligence" and "AI" in official non-statutory documents.

entry.title: Executive Order 14434 — "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence"
entry.mechanism: Full text read (781 words). Terminology order: "to the maximum extent permitted by law, the executive branch shall use the terms 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' and will not acknowledge the usage of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in any applicable setting" (Sec. 1); applies to official correspondence, communications, websites, reports and other non-statutory documents, without altering existing regulations, Presidential actions, contracts or grants (Sec. 2). Definition: "Super Intelligence" means the technologies encompassed by "artificial intelligence" as defined in 15 U.S.C. § 9401(3) (Sec. 3(a)). Within 60 days (by about Nov 28, 2026) the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology must propose legislative language for a federal definition of "Super Intelligence," including whether it should supersede the statutory AI definition and conforming amendments (Sec. 3(b)). Contains no safety, testing, licensing, frontier-model or task-force provision. Signed the same day as the White House accord; it ends the "no new federal AI executive order since EO 14409" finding, but changes no obligation on developers
entry.status_text: Date: Signed Sept 29, 2026; published Oct 2, 2026 (91 FR 63129)

Within 60 days (by about Nov 28, 2026) the Assistant to the President for Science and Technology must propose legislative language for a federal definition of "Super Intelligence," including whether it should supersede the statutory AI definition and conforming amendments (Sec. 3(b)). Contains no safety, testing, licensing, frontier-model or task-force provision. Signed the same day as the White House accord; it ends the "no new federal AI executive order since EO 14409" finding, but changes no obligation on developers

draft.summary_line: Challenges Colorado's SB 24-205 algorithmic-discrimination law, with xAI suing to block it and the Department of Justice intervening on an Equal Protection theory.

entry.title: X.AI LLC v. Weiser, No. 1:26-cv-01515 (D. Colo.)
entry.mechanism: The only federal-state AI litigation located as of Oct 31, 2026 targets a consequential-decision law, not catastrophic-risk regulation; the legal theories used (Equal Protection, compelled speech) do not map cleanly onto SB 53-style disclosure mandates. Also a precedent: DOJ chose to ride a private suit rather than file its own
entry.status_text: Status: xAI sued Apr 9, 2026 to enjoin Colorado SB 24-205 (the ADMT/algorithmic-discrimination law — Section I, not a frontier law) on First Amendment, Equal Protection, and dormant Commerce Clause grounds. DOJ intervened Apr 24, 2026 (Civil Rights Division; Equal Protection theory) — the first federal court action against any state AI law. On Apr 27, 2026 the court granted the parties' joint stipulation: the Colorado AG may not initiate enforcement, including investigations, of SB 24-205 (or legislation replacing or amending it) for conduct on or before 14 days after a ruling on xAI's forthcoming preliminary-injunction motion, which xAI must file within 28 days after final adoption of implementing rules; all case deadlines are stayed; the legislature then repealed and replaced it with SB 26-189 (May 14, 2026)

draft.summary_line: Anthropic challenges its federal supply-chain-risk designation and related measures; the court granted summary judgment largely for Anthropic and the government has appealed.

entry.title: Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Department of War et al., No. 3:26-cv-01996 (N.D. Cal.)
entry.short_name: Anthropic v. Department of War (N.D. Cal.)
entry.mechanism: First direct court challenge in the tracker involving federal treatment of a frontier-model developer. It concerns procurement, national-security designation, and alleged retaliation — not the validity of a state frontier statute. Legally notable for the paper: the complaint pleads that a "supply chain risk" designation under § 3252 had never before been applied to a domestic company
entry.status_text: Status: Complaint read. Filed Mar. 9, 2026 (WilmerHale; 48 pp.) against DoW, Treasury, FHFA, State, HHS, Commerce, VA, GSA, OPM, NRC, SSA, DHS, SEC, NASA, DOE, the Federal Reserve Board, NEA, the Executive Office of the President, and named officials. Five counts: (I) APA / 10 U.S.C. § 3252 — the supply-chain-risk order exceeds § 3252, which is limited to adversary sabotage/subversion risk, skipped the statute's consultation, written-determination, and congressional-notification steps, and is arbitrary given DoD's simultaneous six-month continued-use order; (II) First Amendment retaliation for protected speech and petitioning; (III) ultra vires presidential directive; (IV) Fifth Amendment due process (de facto debarment without notice or hearing); (V) APA § 558 unauthorized sanctions by other agencies. Seeks vacatur, § 705 stay, declaratory relief, and a permanent injunction. Update: on Aug 27, 2026 Judge Rita F. It concerns procurement, national-security designation, and alleged retaliation — not the validity of a state frontier statute. Legally notable for the paper: the complaint pleads that a "supply chain risk" designation under § 3252 had never before been applied to a domestic company
entry.status_text: Status: Complaint read. Filed Mar. 9, 2026 (WilmerHale; 48 pp.) against DoW, Treasury, FHFA, State, HHS, Commerce, VA, GSA, OPM, NRC, SSA, DHS, SEC, NASA, DOE, the Federal Reserve Board, NEA, the Executive Office of the President, and named officials. Five counts: (I) APA / 10 U.S.C. § 3252 — the supply-chain-risk order exceeds § 3252, which is limited to adversary sabotage/subversion risk, skipped the statute's consultation, written-determination, and congressional-notification steps, and is arbitrary given DoD's simultaneous six-month continued-use order; (II) First Amendment retaliation for protected speech and petitioning; (III) ultra vires presidential directive; (IV) Fifth Amendment due process (de facto debarment without notice or hearing); (V) APA § 558 unauthorized sanctions by other agencies. Seeks vacatur, § 705 stay, declaratory relief, and a permanent injunction. Update: on Aug 27, 2026 Judge Rita F. Lin granted summary judgment largely for Anthropic , holding the § 3252 designation and related measures "illegal and baseless" — First Amendment retaliation, Fifth Amendment due process, and APA violations (in excess of statutory authority; arbitrary and capricious) — while rejecting the ultra vires/separation-of-powers count; concurring accounts state the designation was vacated and its enforcement permanently enjoined, and the docket shows the case closed Aug 27, 2026. The government's earlier Ninth Circuit appeal of the preliminary injunction (No. 26-2011) was stayed Apr 27 pending the D.C. Circuit; the government (defendants) filed a new notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit on Oct 26, 2026 (Dkt. 253; Ninth Circuit number not yet located), appealing the Aug 27, 2026 summary-judgment order, order of final relief and judgment

Five counts: (I) APA / 10 U.S.C. § 3252 — the supply-chain-risk order exceeds § 3252, which is limited to adversary sabotage/subversion risk, skipped the statute's consultation, written-determination, and congressional-notification steps, and is arbitrary given DoD's simultaneous six-month continued-use order; (II) First Amendment retaliation for protected speech and petitioning; (III) ultra vires presidential directive; (IV) Fifth Amendment due process (de facto debarment without notice or hearing); (V) APA § 558 unauthorized sanctions by other agencies. Seeks vacatur, § 705 stay, declaratory relief, and a permanent injunction. Update: on Aug 27, 2026 Judge Rita F. Lin granted summary judgment largely for Anthropic , holding the § 3252 designation and related measures "illegal and baseless" — First Amendment retaliation, Fifth Amendment due process, and APA violations (in excess of statutory authority; arbitrary and capricious) — while rejecting the ultra vires/separation-of-powers count; concurring accounts state the designation was vacated and its enforcement permanently enjoined, and the docket shows the case closed Aug 27, 2026. The government's earlier Ninth Circuit appeal of the preliminary injunction (No. 26-2011) was stayed Apr 27 pending the D.C. Circuit; the government (defendants) filed a new notice of appeal to the Ninth Circuit on Oct 26, 2026 (Dkt. 253; Ninth Circuit number not yet located), appealing the Aug 27, 2026 summary-judgment order, order of final relief and judgment

entry.title: Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Department of War, Nos. 26-1049 and 26-1162 (D.C. Cir.) — petition for review of the 41 U.S.C. § 4713 designation
entry.short_name: Anthropic v. DoW, D.C. Cir. (§ 4713) — petition denied
entry.mechanism: The two statutory designations now have opposite outcomes: § 3252 vacated in N.D. Cal. (Aug. 27), § 4713 upheld in the D.C. Circuit (Sept. 25). The majority reportedly reasoned both rulings can coexist because the two statutes define supply-chain risk differently — the split-forum structure flagged in the Sept. 5 version has produced a split result
entry.status_text: Status: The Mar. 9 complaint (n.36) states Anthropic received a separate Mar. 3 letter invoking 41 U.S.C. § 4713 (civilian-agency supply-chain exclusion), that judicial review lies exclusively in the D.C. Circuit under 41 U.S.C. § 1327(b), and that Anthropic "intends to challenge that separate action in that forum." Update: the petition was in fact filed Mar. 9, 2026 (the earlier "no petition located" finding is superseded); stay denied Apr. 8; argued May 19; decided Sept. 25, 2026, 2–1, petition denied . Katsas (writing) and Rao held that FASCSA's term "manipulate" reaches a contractor that "disable[s] Claude from performing lawful actions requested by the Department," and that the First Amendment claim failed because the exclusion rested on "refusal to assent to a contract term that the Department deemed essential"; Henderson dissented, reading manipulation to require deceptive or covert interference rather than "a contractor's honest and upfront enforcement of restrictions." Anthropic: "considering all options, including further review." In October 2026 Anthropic petitioned for panel rehearing or rehearing en banc (reported as filed Oct 13; an amicus motion filed Oct 20, 2026 in No. 26-1049 confirms the petition); no ruling located as of Oct 31, 2026

entry.title: Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Department of War, Nos. 26-1049 and 26-1162 (D.C. Cir.) — petition for review of the 41 U.S.C. § 4713 designation
entry.short_name: Anthropic v. DoW, D.C. Cir. (§ 4713) — petition denied
entry.mechanism: The two statutory designations now have opposite outcomes: § 3252 vacated in N.D. Cal. (Aug. 27), § 4713 upheld in the D.C. Circuit (Sept. 25). The majority reportedly reasoned both rulings can coexist because the two statutes define supply-chain risk differently — the split-forum structure flagged in the Sept. 5 version has produced a split result
entry.status_text: Status: The Mar. 9 complaint (n.36) states Anthropic received a separate Mar. 3 letter invoking 41 U.S.C. § 4713 (civilian-agency supply-chain exclusion), that judicial review lies exclusively in the D.C. Circuit under 41 U.S.C. § 1327(b), and that Anthropic "intends to challenge that separate action in that forum." Update: the petition was in fact filed Mar. 9, 2026 (the earlier "no petition located" finding is superseded); stay denied Apr. 8; argued May 19; decided Sept. 25, 2026, 2–1, petition denied . Katsas (writing) and Rao held that FASCSA's term "manipulate" reaches a contractor that "disable[s] Claude from performing lawful actions requested by the Department," and that the First Amendment claim failed because the exclusion rested on "refusal to assent to a contract term that the Department deemed essential"; Henderson dissented, reading manipulation to require deceptive or covert interference rather than "a contractor's honest and upfront enforcement of restrictions." Anthropic: "considering all options, including further review." In October 2026 Anthropic petitioned for panel rehearing or rehearing en banc (reported as filed Oct 13; an amicus motion filed Oct 20, 2026 in No. 26-1049 confirms the petition); no ruling located as of Oct 31, 2026

entry.title: Anthropic PBC v. U.S. Department of War, Nos. 26-1049 and 26-1162 (D.C. Cir.) — petition for review of the 41 U.S.C. § 4713 designation
entry.short_name: Anthropic v. DoW, D.C. Cir. (§ 4713) — petition denied
entry.mechanism: The two statutory designations now have opposite outcomes: § 3252 vacated in N.D. Cal. (Aug. 27), § 4713 upheld in the D.C. Circuit (Sept. 25). The majority reportedly reasoned both rulings can coexist because the two statutes define supply-chain risk differently — the split-forum structure flagged in the Sept. 5 version has produced a split result
entry.status_text: Status: The Mar. 9 complaint (n.36) states Anthropic received a separate Mar. 3 letter invoking 41 U.S.C. § 4713 (civilian-agency supply-chain exclusion), that judicial review lies exclusively in the D.C. Circuit under 41 U.S.C. § 1327(b), and that Anthropic "intends to challenge that separate action in that forum." Update: the petition was in fact filed Mar. 9, 2026 (the earlier "no petition located" finding is superseded); stay denied Apr. 8; argued May 19; decided Sept. 25, 2026, 2–1, petition denied . Katsas (writing) and Rao held that FASCSA's term "manipulate" reaches a contractor that "disable[s] Claude from performing lawful actions requested by the Department," and that the First Amendment claim failed because the exclusion rested on "refusal to assent to a contract term that the Department deemed essential"; Henderson dissented, reading manipulation to require deceptive or covert interference rather than "a contractor's honest and upfront enforcement of restrictions." Anthropic: "considering all options, including further review." In October 2026 Anthropic petitioned for panel rehearing or rehearing en banc (reported as filed Oct 13; an amicus motion filed Oct 20, 2026 in No. 26-1049 confirms the petition); no ruling located as of Oct 31, 2026

Reyes), with a preliminary-injunction motion. Reyes), with a preliminary-injunction motion. It seeks the administration's reportedly finalized Aug. 1 voluntary framework for reviewing closed frontier models before release, participating-company information, and the claimed legal authority. The preliminary-injunction motion seeks disclosure of the unclassified procedural and contractual architecture by Sept 30, 2026. entry.title: State of Florida v. OpenAI — motion for temporary injunction against frontier development (Fla. state court)
entry.mechanism: The first attempt to use a state court injunction, rather than a statute, to condition frontier development on third-party-approved safeguards; the theory tracks the IVO/auditor layer in Section C. Case number not located
entry.status_text: Status: Motion filed Sept 28, 2026 in Highlands County Circuit Court (Tenth Judicial Circuit, Judge Heather Beato) in the suit Florida filed June 1, 2026 alleging violations of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act plus negligent design and marketing, failure to warn and public nuisance over ChatGPT's effects on vulnerable users. OpenAI removed the case to federal court; a federal judge sent it back to Highlands County. The state asks the court to stop OpenAI from continuing to develop a "reckless, unacceptably risky product" without "third-party approved safety guardrails," arguing OpenAI has "repeatedly shown they are incapable of monitoring their AI, and hesitant in revealing rogue activity once discovered," and citing the Hugging Face incident and later misalignment disclosures. No hearing date or ruling reported as of Oct 31, 2026

entry.mechanism: The first attempt to use a state court injunction, rather than a statute, to condition frontier development on third-party-approved safeguards; the theory tracks the IVO/auditor layer in Section C. Case number not located
entry.status_text: Status: Motion filed Sept 28, 2026 in Highlands County Circuit Court (Tenth Judicial Circuit, Judge Heather Beato) in the suit Florida filed June 1, 2026 alleging violations of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act plus negligent design and marketing, failure to warn and public nuisance over ChatGPT's effects on vulnerable users. OpenAI removed the case to federal court; a federal judge sent it back to Highlands County. The state asks the court to stop OpenAI from continuing to develop a "reckless, unacceptably risky product" without "third-party approved safety guardrails," arguing OpenAI has "repeatedly shown they are incapable of monitoring their AI, and hesitant in revealing rogue activity once discovered," and citing the Hugging Face incident and later misalignment disclosures. No hearing date or ruling reported as of Oct 31, 2026

entry.title: GAIN AI Act of 2025 (S.3150)
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Jim Banks (R-IN)
entry.mechanism: BIS must require a license to export, reexport, or transfer covered chips to entities located/headquartered (or whose parent is headquartered) in a country of concern; applicant must certify US persons had a right of first refusal (public notice, not fewer than 15 business days to request), no backlog of US requests or foreseeable backlog over the 12-month period, and no better pricing for foreign persons; license denied without certification; BIS regulations within 90 days; trusted US persons exempt from certain license requirements for non-concern destinations
entry.thresholds: Covered circuit = advanced integrated circuit (ECCN 3A090/4A090 or equivalent, or TPP 4,800 or more; TPP 2,400+ with density 1.6+; TPP 1,600+ with density 3.2+; or DRAM bandwidth 1,400 GB/s, interconnect 1,100 GB/s, or sum 1,700 GB/s) or product containing one, excluding chips not designed or marketed for data centers; country of concern = Country Group D:5 or E, Macau, Hong Kong

entry.mechanism: BIS must require a license to export, reexport, or transfer covered chips to entities located/headquartered (or whose parent is headquartered) in a country of concern; applicant must certify US persons had a right of first refusal (public notice, not fewer than 15 business days to request), no backlog of US requests or foreseeable backlog over the 12-month period, and no better pricing for foreign persons; license denied without certification; BIS regulations within 90 days; trusted US persons exempt from certain license requirements for non-concern destinations
entry.thresholds: Covered circuit = advanced integrated circuit (ECCN 3A090/4A090 or equivalent, or TPP 4,800 or more; TPP 2,400+ with density 1.6+; TPP 1,600+ with density 3.2+; or DRAM bandwidth 1,400 GB/s, interconnect 1,100 GB/s, or sum 1,700 GB/s) or product containing one, excluding chips not designed or marketed for data centers; country of concern = Country Group D:5 or E, Macau, Hong Kong
entry.status_text: Date / status: Introduced in the Senate Nov. 6, 2025; referred to Senate Banking; no further action as of Oct. 31, 2026

thirty_seconds.a: Anyone exporting, reexporting or transferring covered advanced chips to entities located or headquartered in Country Group D:5 or E, Macau or Hong Kong, or whose parent is. Chips not designed or marketed for data centers are excluded. Fines reach $7,777,777.
thirty_seconds.b: The bill would require a license, with a certification that US persons had a right of first refusal, no backlog or foreseeable backlog over 12 months, and no better pricing for foreign buyers.
thirty_seconds.c: The license would be denied without the certification.

draft.summary_line: Traces the 10²⁶ operations reporting trigger for dual-use foundation models from EO 14110 and a BIS proposal to the same benchmark in current state frontier statutes.

entry.title: Documentary lineage of the 10²⁶ threshold
entry.mechanism: EO 14110 §4.2 used 10²⁶ integer/floating-point operations as a reporting trigger for dual-use foundation models; BIS's Sept. 2024 proposal repeated it. Current state frontier statutes use the same numerical benchmark. EO 14110 was revoked Jan. 20, 2025. This establishes documentary lineage, but not that every legislature copied the EO directly. No final version of BIS-2024-0047 was located before the revocation, so that procedural-status point is search-qualified

draft.summary_line: Would require Commerce licences for exports of advanced AI chips to countries of concern, with a 30-day congressional review and disapproval process.

entry.title: AI OVERWATCH Act (H.R. 6875, Rep. Mast; S. 4456, Sen. Banks with Sen. Warren among 10 cosponsors) and other FY2027 NDAA AI provisions
entry.mechanism: Requires Commerce licences for exports of advanced AI chips to countries of concern, with a 30-day congressional review and disapproval mechanism modelled on arms-sales review, and codifies the license denial for the most capable chips, whose technical parameters Commerce may revise only after 18 months; Commerce certification that exports of lesser chips do not divert US supply or foundry capacity or permit unauthorized remote access; an "American AI Victory Strategy." The AIPN conference letter also lists House Sec. 240 (AGI Preparedness Initiative), House Sec. 1502 (AI Incident and Vulnerability Reporting Program), and Senate Secs. 1634 (insider-threat reporting for large AI contractors), 1652–1655 (AI bill of materials, human oversight for use of force, biosecurity procurement for covered AI models, secure AI data centers) as provisions in play
entry.thresholds: Covered integrated circuits (H.R. 6875): ECCN 3A090 or 4A090, or chips with total processing performance of 4,800 or more; 2,400 or more with performance density of 1.6 or more; 1,600 or more with density of 3.2 or more; or DRAM bandwidth of 1,400 gigabytes per second or more, interconnect 1,100 gigabytes per second or more, or combined 1,700 gigabytes per second; excludes chips not designed or marketed for data centers
entry.status_text: Date / status: H.R. 6875 introduced Dec 18, 2025 and ordered reported in the nature of a substitute by House Foreign Affairs 42–2 on Jan 21, 2026; S. 4456 introduced Apr 30, 2026; in the Senate NDAA manager's package as SA 6575 (submitted July 13, 2026; S. 4784 itself was reported June 15, 2026) ; Senate NDAA (S. 4784) awaiting floor action after a failed cloture vote July 14; House NDAA (H.R. 8800) passed July 22, received in the Senate Sept 14, 2026; the Senate has not passed its NDAA, so there is no conference yet
