draft.summary_line: Describes would require Commerce licences for exports of advanced AI chips to countries of concern, with a 30-day congressional review and disapproval process.

entry.title: AI OVERWATCH Act (H.R. 6875, Rep. Mast; S. 4456, Sen. Banks with Sen. Warren among 10 cosponsors) and other FY2027 NDAA AI provisions
entry.mechanism: Requires Commerce licences for exports of advanced AI chips to countries of concern, with a 30-day congressional review and disapproval mechanism modelled on arms-sales review, and codifies the license denial for the most capable chips, whose technical parameters Commerce may revise only after 18 months; Commerce certification that exports of lesser chips do not divert US supply or foundry capacity or permit unauthorized remote access; an "American AI Victory Strategy." The AIPN conference letter also lists House Sec. 240 (AGI Preparedness Initiative), House Sec. 1502 (AI Incident and Vulnerability Reporting Program), and Senate Secs. 1634 (insider-threat reporting for large AI contractors), 1652–1655 (AI bill of materials, human oversight for use of force, biosecurity procurement for covered AI models, secure AI data centers) as provisions in play
entry.thresholds: Covered integrated circuits (H.R. 6875): ECCN 3A090 or 4A090, or chips with total processing performance of 4,800 or more; 2,400 or more with performance density of 1.6 or more; 1,600 or more with density of 3.2 or more; or DRAM bandwidth of 1,400 gigabytes per second or more, interconnect 1,100 gigabytes per second or more, or combined 1,700 gigabytes per second; excludes chips not designed or marketed for data centers

entry.title: AI OVERWATCH Act (H.R. 6875, Rep. Mast; S. 4456, Sen. Banks with Sen. Warren among 10 cosponsors) and other FY2027 NDAA AI provisions
entry.mechanism: Requires Commerce licences for exports of advanced AI chips to countries of concern, with a 30-day congressional review and disapproval mechanism modelled on arms-sales review, and codifies the license denial for the most capable chips, whose technical parameters Commerce may revise only after 18 months; Commerce certification that exports of lesser chips do not divert US supply or foundry capacity or permit unauthorized remote access; an "American AI Victory Strategy." The AIPN conference letter also lists House Sec. 240 (AGI Preparedness Initiative), House Sec. 1502 (AI Incident and Vulnerability Reporting Program), and Senate Secs. 1634 (insider-threat reporting for large AI contractors), 1652–1655 (AI bill of materials, human oversight for use of force, biosecurity procurement for covered AI models, secure AI data centers) as provisions in play
entry.thresholds: Covered integrated circuits (H.R. 6875): ECCN 3A090 or 4A090, or chips with total processing performance of 4,800 or more; 2,400 or more with performance density of 1.6 or more; 1,600 or more with density of 3.2 or more; or DRAM bandwidth of 1,400 gigabytes per second or more, interconnect 1,100 gigabytes per second or more, or combined 1,700 gigabytes per second; excludes chips not designed or marketed for data centers

entry.title: S.B. 1047 — Safe and Secure Innovation for Frontier AI Models Act
entry.mechanism: The enrolled bill required covered developers to implement a written safety and security protocol, retain an annual independent auditor, submit compliance certifications before training/deployment, maintain a full-shutdown capability, and report safety incidents. entry.title: California ballot initiative A.G. File No. 25-0034, Amendment #1 — "Regulates Certain Large Artificial Intelligence (AI) Companies. Initiative Statute."
entry.mechanism: LAO analysis (Jan 20, 2026) read: would create an independent seven-member California AI Safety Commission regulating "frontier AI companies" defined by valuation, capital raised, or expenditures plus a commission-set capability threshold (no FLOP number) ; registration; review of protection plans covering workforce displacement, safety, and loss of control; authority to delay capability expansions ; emergency orders; certification of independent evaluators; civil fines up to 20% of California revenue; executives personally liable up to $1M; felony penalties (2–6 years); private enforcement ; funded by registrant fees up to 0.5% of CA revenue. The maximal SB 1047-style design, attempted via direct democracy
entry.status_text: Status: Withdrawn Feb 27, 2026 (confirmed on CA AG inactive-measures page; title and summary had issued Feb 4, 2026; proponent Alexander Oldham). Companion initiative 25-0033 — regulating AI public-benefit corporations and nonprofits — withdrawn the same day

entry.title: S.B. 5 — "An Act Concerning Online Safety" (Public Act 26-15; called the "C.A.R.T. Act" by its sponsors)
entry.mechanism: 39-section omnibus (AEDT/employment AI incl. WARN-notice AI disclosure, companion chatbots, provenance, social media, regulatory sandbox). Frontier-relevant sections: "frontier developer" = doing business in CT + >10²⁶ FLOPs; "large frontier developer" = >$500M revenue; frontier developers may not retaliate against employees reporting catastrophic-risk concerns (effective Oct. 1, 2026 ); large frontier developers must operate anonymous internal reporting channels by Jan. 1, 2027 ; civil penalty up to $1,000 per violation for the whistleblower duties, in an AG action in Hartford superior court ; plus a DCP-run IVO pilot through June 30, 2030 — see Section C . No developer framework, transparency-report, incident-reporting, or audit mandate. Reports go to officers/directors quarterly unless alleging their wrongdoing; AG also recovers fees.
entry.status_text: Status: Passed May 1, 2026 (Senate 32–4, House 131–17); signed May 27, 2026 ; the employment-AI sections (Secs. 8–11) are enforced solely by the AG under CUTPA with a 60-day cure period through 2027

Frontier-relevant sections: "frontier developer" = doing business in CT + >10²⁶ FLOPs; "large frontier developer" = >$500M revenue; frontier developers may not retaliate against employees reporting catastrophic-risk concerns (effective Oct. 1, 2026 ); large frontier developers must operate anonymous internal reporting channels by Jan. 1, 2027 ; civil penalty up to $1,000 per violation for the whistleblower duties, in an AG action in Hartford superior court ; plus a DCP-run IVO pilot through June 30, 2030 — see Section C . No developer framework, transparency-report, incident-reporting, or audit mandate. Reports go to officers/directors quarterly unless alleging their wrongdoing; AG also recovers fees.

draft.summary_line: Would require large AI contractors with Department of Defense contracts to report insider-threat protections and notify DoD within 72 hours of acute national security risks.

entry.title: S. 5601 — Insider Threat Reporting and Security Guidance Act of 2026
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Jim Banks (R-IN), sponsor; Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), original cosponsor
entry.mechanism: Sectoral (DoD). Within 180 days DoD issues regulations requiring large AI contractors to report their personnel vetting, insider-threat, access-control and model-weight theft protections with every bid, and to re-certify every 90 days; they must notify DoD within 72 hours of any acute national security risk (model-weight theft, exfiltration, poisoning, "materially concerning model behavior" such as cyber-offense uplift, deception or unauthorized autonomous action), and DoD tells the Armed Services committees within 7 days. DoD forwards incident notices to, among others, the NSA's Artificial Intelligence Security Center. Also voluntary insider-threat guidance for these contractors
entry.thresholds: DoD AI contracts worth at least $100,000,000, and at least $1,000,000,000 in AI R&D over the prior 3 years (with affiliates), or use of a model from a developer that meets that spending test

entry.title: H.R. 3919 — Advanced AI Security Readiness Act
entry.short_name: H.R. 3919 Advanced AI Security Readiness Act
entry.sponsor_text: Rep. Darin LaHood (R-IL), 8 co-sponsors
entry.mechanism: The NSA, through its AI Security Center, writes an "AI Security Playbook" to defend covered AI technologies from theft by nation-state and other highly resourced actors: vulnerabilities at advanced AI developers and data centers, which components (models, weights, core insights) matter most, and the security levels that would need substantial US Government involvement, including a hypothetical secure government build. NSA must engage prominent AI developers and review their preparedness frameworks and scaling policies. Initial report in 90 days, final in 270 days, with a public version; no regulatory or enforcement authority
entry.thresholds: Capability-based, no compute figure: "covered AI technologies" are advanced AI with critical capabilities that would pose a grave national security threat if stolen, such as systems that match or exceed human expert performance in CBRN, cyber offense, model autonomy, persuasion, R&D and self-improvement

draft.summary_line: Would require the Secretary of Defense to set up an Artificial General Intelligence Steering Committee to study AGI and its military uses and report to Congress.

entry.title: S. 2604 — Artificial General Intelligence Steering Committee (Department of Defense)
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Mike Rounds (R-SD), sponsor; Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) added as cosponsor Nov 20, 2025
entry.mechanism: Sectoral (DoD), no duties on developers. By April 1, 2026 the Secretary of Defense establishes an "Artificial General Intelligence Steering Committee", co-chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, to analyze the trajectory of AI models toward artificial general intelligence (including frontier and world models and agentic algorithms), adversaries' progress toward AGI, military applications, a DoD adoption strategy with "ethical and policy guardrails", and counter-AGI strategies; report to the congressional defense committees by January 31, 2027 (unclassified portion public, classified annex allowed); sunsets December 31, 2027

entry.sponsor_text: Rep. Joseph Ciresi (D) with 13 co-sponsors, including Republicans Jason Ortitay and Andrea Verobish

entry.title: S.10731 — Amendments to the RAISE Act (responsible AI safety and education act)
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Gounardes with co-sponsor Sen. Fahy
entry.mechanism: Introduced text read. Amends the RAISE Act (GBL Article 44-B as added by Chapter 96 of 2026): the frontier AI framework must also cover security risk, the automation of AI research and development, internal use, models evading training or assessment, and models used to monitor other models (§ 1421(1)), and the office may add framework elements by regulation (§ 1421(2)); the office must adopt binding minimum standards for frameworks and mitigations by January 1, 2029 (§ 1422); transparency reports add the model specification and how reproducible assessments are (§ 1421(4)); an accountable senior officer certifies publications and submissions under penalty of perjury (§ 1421(5)); measures to prevent and contain critical safety incidents (§ 1421(6)); a wider critical safety incident definition (§ 1420(5)); assessments of internal-use risk, AI research automation and compute use go to the office every three months and within 72 hours of a substantial increase, shared with the Attorney General (§ 1423(2)); critical safety incident reports within 72 hours, and within 24 hours to an appropriate authority for imminent risk of death or serious physical injury (§ 1423(3)); an annual frontier examiner compliance report plus continuous examination with reports every 90 days from April 1, 2028, examiner independence rules, and licensed examiners only from January 1, 2029 (§ 1424); examiner covered-emergency reports within 72 hours (§ 1424(7)); the office may order large frontier developers to limit compute used to train new models or for automated research and development (§ 1425); whistleblower protections tied to Labor Law § 740 (§ 1426); Attorney General civil penalties up to $1,000,000 per day of a first violation and $3,000,000 per day of a subsequent violation, plus injunctions that may restrict a model's deployment in the state (§ 1431); no private right of action
entry.thresholds: Frontier model = trained on more than 10²⁵ operations (lowered from 10²⁶), counting fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, or a foundation model the office determines is among the most capable, poses catastrophic risk and is reasonably likely to automate AI research and development (§ 1420(12)); large frontier developer = more than $1,000,000,000 in frontier-model expenditures with affiliates over the preceding 36 months, replacing the $500,000,000 revenue test (§ 1420(14)); catastrophic risk = death or serious injury to more than 50 people or more than $1,000,000,000 in property damage from a single incident or multiple incidents (§ 1420(3))

entry.title: S.10731 — Amendments to the RAISE Act (responsible AI safety and education act)
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Gounardes with co-sponsor Sen. Fahy
entry.mechanism: Introduced text read. entry.title: S.10731 — Amendments to the RAISE Act (responsible AI safety and education act)
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Gounardes with co-sponsor Sen. Fahy
entry.mechanism: Introduced text read. Amends the RAISE Act (GBL Article 44-B as added by Chapter 96 of 2026): the frontier AI framework must also cover security risk, the automation of AI research and development, internal use, models evading training or assessment, and models used to monitor other models (§ 1421(1)), and the office may add framework elements by regulation (§ 1421(2)); the office must adopt binding minimum standards for frameworks and mitigations by January 1, 2029 (§ 1422); transparency reports add the model specification and how reproducible assessments are (§ 1421(4)); an accountable senior officer certifies publications and submissions under penalty of perjury (§ 1421(5)); measures to prevent and contain critical safety incidents (§ 1421(6)); a wider critical safety incident definition (§ 1420(5)); assessments of internal-use risk, AI research automation and compute use go to the office every three months and within 72 hours of a substantial increase, shared with the Attorney General (§ 1423(2)); critical safety incident reports within 72 hours, and within 24 hours to an appropriate authority for imminent risk of death or serious physical injury (§ 1423(3)); an annual frontier examiner compliance report plus continuous examination with reports every 90 days from April 1, 2028, examiner independence rules, and licensed examiners only from January 1, 2029 (§ 1424); examiner covered-emergency reports within 72 hours (§ 1424(7)); the office may order large frontier developers to limit compute used to train new models or for automated research and development (§ 1425); whistleblower protections tied to Labor Law § 740 (§ 1426); Attorney General civil penalties up to $1,000,000 per day of a first violation and $3,000,000 per day of a subsequent violation, plus injunctions that may restrict a model's deployment in the state (§ 1431); no private right of action
entry.thresholds: Frontier model = trained on more than 10²⁵ operations (lowered from 10²⁶), counting fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, or a foundation model the office determines is among the most capable, poses catastrophic risk and is reasonably likely to automate AI research and development (§ 1420(12)); large frontier developer = more than $1,000,000,000 in frontier-model expenditures with affiliates over the preceding 36 months, replacing the $500,000,000 revenue test (§ 1420(14)); catastrophic risk = death or serious injury to more than 50 people or more than $1,000,000,000 in property damage from a single incident or multiple incidents (§ 1420(3))

entry.mechanism: Introduced text read (Printer's No. 4002, 25 pp.; co-sponsorship memo titled "Pennsylvania Advanced Artificial Intelligence Accountability and Innovation Act"). Free-standing act on the SB 53 pattern with a disclosure layer: from January 1, 2028 large frontier developers file an annual disclosure statement with ownership information with the Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency (PEMA) and pay a pro rata fee (Sec. 104); write, implement, comply with and publish a frontier AI framework from January 1, 2028, reviewed at least annually, sent to PEMA and the Attorney General, and re-published within 30 days of a material modification (Secs. 501–503); annual independent third-party audit with independence limits, summary and redacted report published within 30 days (Sec. 504); internal-use risk assessment summaries to PEMA every three months (Sec. 505); a ban on deploying a frontier model that would create an unreasonable risk of catastrophic harm (Sec. 506); transparency reports before deployment, with summaries in machine-readable format (Sec. 701); critical safety incident reports to PEMA and the Attorney General within 72 hours, and within 24 hours to an appropriate authority for imminent risk of death or serious physical injury (Sec. 702); whistleblower protections preserving the state Whistleblower Law (Sec. 1103); civil penalties up to $1,000,000 for a first violation and $3,000,000 per subsequent violation, recovered by the Attorney General, plus PEMA penalties of $1,000 per day after notice and hearing for disclosure failures (Secs. 104(d), 1105); preemption of local frontier-model rules (Sec. 1107); no private right of action
entry.thresholds: Frontier model = trained on more than 10²⁶ operations, counting the original run and subsequent fine-tuning and reinforcement learning; large frontier developer = more than $500,000,000 annual gross revenue with affiliates; catastrophic risk = death or serious injury to more than 50 people or more than $1,000,000,000 in property damage from a single incident (Sec. 102)

entry.title: HB 4098 — artificial intelligence business; attorney general
entry.short_name: AZ HB 4098 AI business; attorney general
entry.sponsor_text: Rep. Travers
entry.mechanism: Introduced text read (2026, Fifty-seventh Legislature, Second Regular Session). Would add A.R.S. 44-1383: an "artificial intelligence business" (one whose public-facing AI systems use a frontier model owned or operated by a large developer) must run a comprehensive risk assessment of each high risk AI system before use or sale, covering bias, safety risks to children, privacy and catastrophic risks; submit a transparency report to the Attorney General and post it on its website; adopt bias mitigation measures; run a quarterly audit; give child-accessible systems parental monitoring tools and content filtering; and obtain an Attorney General certification before entering the stream of commerce. The Attorney General enforces, with civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation, each day a separate violation
entry.thresholds: Frontier model = trained using greater than 10^26 computational operations (printed "10.26") at costs of more than $100,000,000, or by knowledge distillation of a frontier model; large developer = has trained a frontier model and spent more than $5,000,000 developing and more than $100,000,000 training it, excluding accredited colleges and universities doing academic research (A.R.S. 44-1383(K))

entry.title: S 735 — AI Innovation Trust Fund
entry.short_name: NC S 735 AI Innovation Trust Fund
entry.sponsor_text: Sens. Salvador, Garrett and Murdock (primary sponsors)
entry.mechanism: First edition read (2025 Session). Creates the North Carolina Artificial Intelligence Innovation Trust Fund in the Department of Commerce (grants for AI companies, $750,000 appropriated for 2025-26) and, in the same Part, SB 1047-style duties for developers of covered models: before training, cybersecurity protections, full-shutdown capability, a written safety and security protocol implemented as written, retained five years, reviewed annually and published in redacted form to the Attorney General (G.S. 143B-472.83B(c)); pre-deployment assessment of critical-harm capability, test records and safeguards (83B(d)); a ban on use or release with an unreasonable risk of critical harm (83B(e)); an annual independent third-party compliance investigation (83B(g)); an annual signed statement of compliance to the Attorney General (83B(h)); safety incident reports within 72 hours (83B(i)); know-your-customer and shutdown duties for computing-cluster operators (83C); Attorney General enforcement with penalties tied to training compute cost (83D); whistleblower protections and an anonymous internal process (83E); Secretary of Commerce regulations and annual threshold updates (83)
entry.thresholds: Covered model = an AI model the Secretary of Commerce identifies as warranting oversight, considering computing power, training cost, scope and foreseeable risks; covered model derivative includes fine-tuning with up to 3 x 10^25 operations costing over $10,000,000; computing cluster = at least 10^20 operations per second; critical harm = mass casualties from CBRN weapons, or mass casualties or at least $500,000,000 of damage from cyberattacks on critical infrastructure or autonomous crime-like conduct (G.S. 143B-472.83A(b))

entry.title: L.B. 1083 — Transparency in Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Act
entry.short_name: NE L.B. 1083 Transparency in AI Risk Management Act
entry.sponsor_text: Sen. Tanya Storer (District 43), with Sen. Bosn (District 25)
entry.mechanism: Introduced text read (109th Legislature, Second Session). SB 53-pattern act with a child-safety layer for large chatbot providers: large frontier developers and large chatbot providers must write, implement, comply with and publish a "public safety and child protection plan" and re-publish it within thirty days of a material modification (Sec. 4(1)–(2)); large frontier developers publish summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments before or when deploying a new or substantially modified frontier model (Sec. 4(4)); no materially false or misleading statements about covered risks (Sec. 4(5)); frontier developers report critical safety incidents to the Attorney General within fifteen days, and within twenty-four hours to an appropriate authority for imminent risk of death or serious physical injury; large chatbot providers report child safety incidents within fifteen days; large frontier developers send the Attorney General internal-use catastrophic-risk assessment summaries every three months (Sec. 5); the Attorney General may update the coverage definitions by rule (Sec. 6); whistleblower protections with an anonymous internal process at large frontier developers and a private civil action (Sec. 7); Attorney General enforcement with civil penalties up to one million dollars per violation for large frontier developers and fifty thousand dollars for large chatbot providers (Sec. 8); creates a Juvenile Mental Health Support Fund (Sec. 10); public-records exemption for submitted summaries and disclosures (Sec. 11). Operative January 1, 2027 (Sec. 12). Committee amendment AM2618 not read
entry.thresholds: Frontier model = foundation model trained on more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, counting fine-tuning and reinforcement learning; large frontier developer = collective annual revenue of five hundred million dollars or more with affiliates; large chatbot provider = covered chatbot (at least one million monthly active users, foreseeably likely to be accessed by minors) and annual revenue of twenty-five million dollars or more; catastrophic risk = death or serious injury to more than fifty people or more than one billion dollars in property damage from a single incident (Sec. 3)

entry.title: H.B. 25-1212 — Public Safety Protection from the Risks of Artificial Intelligence Systems (whistleblower protections for AI workers)
entry.short_name: CO H.B. 25-1212 AI Worker Whistleblower Protections
entry.sponsor_text: Reps. Rutinel and Soper (House sponsors); no Senate sponsor on the introduced text
entry.mechanism: Introduced text read. Whistleblower-only bill aimed at developers that have trained a foundation model at a computational cost of at least one hundred million dollars (new C.R.S. title 8, article 13.6): developers may not prevent or retaliate against workers (employees, independent contractors, corporate officers) who disclose information about non-compliance with public-safety law, substantial risks to public safety or security, or false or misleading safety statements (8-13.6-102(1)); contracts limiting such disclosures are void (8-13.6-102(3)); notice of rights to all workers on a foundation model (8-13.6-103); an anonymous internal reporting process with monthly updates, records kept seven years and shared quarterly with officers and directors (8-13.6-104); private civil action with reinstatement, the greater of ten thousand dollars or lost pay, punitive damages and attorney fees (8-13.6-105). No safety framework, reporting or audit duties
entry.thresholds: Developer = employer (or entity contracting with five or more independent contractors in the state each year) that has trained at least one foundation model at a computational cost of at least one hundred million dollars, measured by the average cost of equivalent cloud computing when training starts (8-13.6-101(2))

entry.title: A.8833 — Understanding Artificial Intelligence Act (strict liability for covered-model developers)
entry.sponsor_text: Assemblymember Alex Bores (D), with co-sponsor Assemblymember Simone; no Senate same-as bill listed
entry.mechanism: Introduced text read. Adds GBL Article 45-A (§§ 1510–1512). Except for defamation claims, developers of covered models are strictly liable, regardless of the degree of care exercised, for injuries to a non-user of the model that meet the actual harm element of a negligence claim, if the model engaged in conduct that would be negligence or an intentional tort or crime if done by an adult human of sound mind, and the conduct was neither intended nor reasonably anticipated by the user or by an intermediary that fine-tuned, scaffolded or modified the model (§ 1512(1)). Rebuttable presumption that the AI system had the relevant mental state where a natural person acting similarly would have; it is no defense that AI systems cannot have mental states (§ 1512(2)). Affirmative defenses: the model met the human standard of care for the same function, or the injury was a capabilities failure (§ 1512(3)). No framework, reporting, audit or agency duties
entry.thresholds: Covered model = trained using more than 10²⁶ integer or floating-point operations, the cost of which exceeds $100 million at average cloud compute market prices at the start of training (§ 1511(2)); developer = the person that performs the initial training of a covered model (§ 1511(3))
entry.penalties: No fines; civil strict liability to injured non-users (§ 1512)
